young.html: Ludwig Wittgenstein (say VIT-gen-shtine) was an Austrian thinker who taught at Cambridge in England. He wondered about something we do every day: how do words mean things?

You might think every word is a name for a thing, like "apple" for an apple. But what thing does "hello" name? Or "maybe"? Or "ouch"? Wittgenstein said words are more like tools in a toolbox: a hammer, a saw, a ruler, glue. Each does a different job. To know what a word means, watch how people use it.

young.name: gb-witt-builders
young.cap: Wittgenstein imagined two builders with a language of just four words. Call out a word and see what the helper does.

young.html: The word game. Choose a word like "game," "chair" or "fun." Try to write a definition that fits every example and nothing else. Then have someone try to find an example that breaks your definition. Is it harder than you thought?

full.html: Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951) came from one of the richest families in Vienna. He studied with Bertrand Russell at Cambridge, served in the Austrian army in the First World War, and in 1921 published the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, a short, severe book that pictured language as a mirror of facts. He then left philosophy for years, working as a village schoolteacher and a gardener. Back at Cambridge from 1929, he came to think his first book was badly mistaken. Philosophical Investigations, his answer to it, was published in 1953, two years after his death.
No excerpts here. The Investigations was first published in 1953, in German with an English translation, and is under copyright. This lesson describes it in our own words. It is in most libraries.
The book opens with a passage from Augustine's Confessions (earlier on this ladder), in which Augustine remembers how he learned to speak as a child:

full.text: When they named any thing, and as they spoke turned towards it, I saw and remembered that they called what they would point out, by the name they uttered.
full.author: Augustine
full.ed: John Henry Parker, Oxford (Library of the Fathers)

full.html: Here, Wittgenstein says, is a picture of language: words name objects, and sentences combine names. He grants it fits some words. But it leaves out most of what language does.

He imagines two builders. One calls out "block," "pillar," "slab" or "beam," and the other brings that stone. That is a complete language for them, a language game. Our own language is a crowd of such games: giving orders, describing, telling stories, guessing riddles, thanking, greeting, praying, making jokes. The meaning of a word, in many cases, is its use in the language.

full.name: gb-witt-builders
full.cap: The builders' language game (our drawing of Wittgenstein's example).

full.html: What do all games have in common? Board games, card games, ball games, a child throwing a ball at a wall? Instead of assuming there must be something in common, Wittgenstein says, go and look. You find many overlapping similarities but no single feature they all share, the way members of a family share a chin here, eyes there. He calls this family resemblance. Many useful words work this way and have no neat definition.

full.name: gb-witt-games
full.cap: Tap a game to see its features. Look for one feature every game shares. (Our own list, in the spirit of Wittgenstein's example.)

full.html: How do we know what it means to follow a rule, like "add 2"? No rule can contain instructions for its own use; in the end, Wittgenstein argues, following a rule is a practice, something we do together, trained into us. That leads to his famous private language argument: a language whose words referred only to one person's private sensations, understood by no one else, could not work, because there would be no difference between using a word correctly and merely seeming to.

Many philosophical puzzles, Wittgenstein thought, arise when we take words out of the everyday games where they work and make them do something strange. Philosophy's task is to describe how language is really used, so that the puzzle dissolves. His image is a fly trapped in a glass bottle, buzzing against the sides: the philosopher's job is to show it the way out.

The Investigations is often ranked among the most important philosophy books of the 20th century. It shaped "ordinary language" philosophy at Oxford, and later work in linguistics, the philosophy of mind and the social sciences. Critics have argued that it dismisses real philosophical problems as confusions too quickly, that its loose, numbered remarks leave its arguments open to many readings, and, in Saul Kripke's famous 1982 interpretation, that the rule-following argument leads to a startling skepticism Wittgenstein may not have intended. Scholars still disagree about what exactly the book claims.
Thinking "meaning is use" means a word can mean anything anyone likes. Use is shared and governed by the practices of a community; that is the point of the private language argument.

items: Augustine, whose picture of language opens the book.
Plato's dialogues often ask "what is courage?" or "what is justice?" and look for one definition; family resemblance questions whether there always is one.
Russell, his teacher, analysed language with logic; the Investigations turns away from that method.
Heidegger and Wittgenstein were born the same year and both thought philosophy had been misled by language, though in very different ways.
